title: Pressure-cooker black beans
subtitle: Rich, earthy beans ready in 30 minutes from dry
excerpt: Dried black beans cooked under pressure without soaking. Deeply flavoured with aromatics, they are a versatile base for burritos, rice dishes, soups, and dips.
sourceNotes: Black beans are central to Caribbean, Mexican, and South American cooking. Pressure-cooking from dried is the standard home method in those culinary traditions. Cuban black bean soup, feijoada, and refried black beans all start here.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool and freeze in portions in their cooking liquid for up to 6 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Cook a large batch and freeze in 400 g portions, equivalent to one tin of black beans.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps refrigerated in cooking liquid for up to 5 days.

content.text: Black beans have a naturally rich, earthy flavour that comes through particularly well when cooked from dried rather than tinned. The pressure cooker brings them to tender in about 30 minutes with no soaking required. The cooking liquid turns a deep purple-black and is starchy and intensely flavoured, it belongs in the dish, not down the drain.

Adding cumin and garlic to the cooking water seasons the beans from the inside as they absorb the liquid under pressure. This is the Latin American approach, the beans themselves become flavoured rather than just being cooked plain and seasoned afterwards.
Salt only after cooking. Acid, lime juice, tomatoes, vinegar, goes in only at the end or at the table. Both will toughen skins and prevent the beans cooking evenly.

Put the rinsed black beans in the pressure cooker. Add cold water to cover by at least 5 cm, they expand as they cook. Add the bruised garlic, cumin, bay leaf, and olive oil. Do not add salt. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 30 minutes. Allow a full natural pressure release of at least 20 minutes before opening.

Taste a bean, it should be soft all the way through with no powdery centre. If still firm, cook at high pressure for a further 10 minutes. Once cooked, season well with salt and stir. Use immediately or cool in the cooking liquid before storing.

rows.symptom: The beans are tough after 30 minutes
rows.cause: Old beans, or the pot did not reach full pressure.
rows.fix: Cook for a further 10 to 15 minutes. Very old dried beans can take up to 45 minutes.

rows.symptom: The cooking liquid is much lighter than expected
rows.cause: This is normal when the beans are very fresh.
rows.fix: No action needed, the flavour is the same. The liquid darkens more with older or more robust bean varieties.

rows.cause: The cooker was overfilled. Dried legumes expand considerably and produce foam.
rows.fix: Never fill more than half the pot's maximum fill line with dried beans and water. Clean the pressure release valve after cooking.

content.text: Black beans are the foundation of some of the most flavourful dishes in Latin American and Caribbean cooking: feijoada, arroz con frijoles negros, refried black beans, and the Cuban black bean soup that can constitute a meal on its own. Cooked from dried and seasoned well, they are better than any tinned version. Keep a batch in the fridge and use it across the week, in tacos, on rice, in burritos, or simply mashed with olive oil and a squeeze of lime.
